title: Senior Leader of the Sinaloa Cartel and One of FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives Arrested in Mexico Following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation
body: Press Release Senior Leader of the Sinaloa Cartel and One of FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives Arrested in Mexico Following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Saturday, November 21, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs OAG Fausto Isidro Meza Flores , also known as “Chapo Isidro,” an alleged leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, has been captured by the Mexican military following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation. “We commend Mexico’s military and special forces on last night’s capture of Sinaloa Cartel senior leader ‘Chapo Isidro,’ said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “A combined interagency effort, including the Homeland Security Task Force, supported this Mexican operation to remove a leader of one of the most dangerous drug cartels in Mexico. This successful operation is the result of a bilateral effort to eliminate terrorists in Mexico. We extend our condolences to the families of the elite soldiers who were killed and our gratitude to the Mexican government.” “The arrest of Chapo Isidro demonstrates the outstanding strength and reach of the Homeland Security Task Force,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and our HSTF partners relentlessly pursued one of the world’s most dangerous cartel leaders, whose organization is alleged to have flooded our communities with deadly narcotics and terrorized communities through extreme violence. This operation sends an unmistakable message, cartel leaders cannot hide behind borders, money, or brutality. The Homeland Security Task Force will continue its work to dismantle these criminal and terrorist networks, hold their leaders accountable, and protect the American people.” Meza Flores was captured on November 20 in a spectacular military operation in Guasave, Sinaloa, Mexico, that also resulted in the arrest of alleged cartel leader German Rolando Galvez Meza, also known as “El Serafin.” A federal grand jury in the District of Columbia returned a second superseding indictment on September 25 charging Meza-Flores, 44, of Sonora, Mexico, with conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, conducting a continuing criminal enterprise, money laundering and firearms related charges. The case is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California and the Justice Department’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section. The Sinaloa Cartel is one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities. On February 20, 2025, the U.S. Secretary of State designated the Cartel de Sinaloa as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) under Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act and as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist under Executive Order 13224. The Secretary of State has also listed the following aliases for the Cartel de Sinaloa: Sinaloa Cartel, Mexican Federation, and Guadalajara Cartel. According to court documents, under Meza Flores’s leadership, the Sinaloa Cartel produced and trafficked multi-tonnage quantities of drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl into the United States, and used extreme violence to further its operations. Meza Flores commanded a large contingent of gunmen to control significant territory in the Guasave, Los Mochis, and remote Sinaloa mountains. The cartel uses this territory to manufacture and distribute illicit controlled substances, transporting them north to the United States. It is further alleged that Meza Flores has engaged in continual and extreme violence, including (1) murdering rival cartel members in public; (2) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering rival cartel members at camps and elsewhere; (3) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering members of the Mexican police; and (4) terrorizing the people of Mexico. “Meza Flores is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives List for a reason; he is the most dangerous man in Mexico,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa Cartel, promoting unparalleled violence throughout southern Mexico and flooding the United States with deadly substances all in the name of profit. With this indictment made possible by the Homeland Security Task Force, subsequent arrest and the continued support of our Mexican partners, we aim to bring him to justice and fully dismantle this cartel.” “Chapo Isidro built an empire in the shadows. Today’s sunrise was his sunset,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California. “Another FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive is off the board,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” has been captured by Mexican forces with U.S. assistance. This alleged cartel leader is accused of flooding American communities with deadly drugs, including fentanyl. This is the 11th Ten Most Wanted fugitive captured under the Trump Administration. Outstanding work by our law enforcement partners in Mexico and everyone involved in this operation. Under President Trump’s leadership, this FBI will continue relentlessly pursuing the criminals and cartels poisoning our communities and threatening American lives.” “Homeland Security Investigations is proud of the exceptional work of our special agents and personnel across our domestic and international offices whose determination, expertise, and coordination through the HSTF helped bring Chapo Isidro to justice,” said HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Working alongside our HSTF partners, HSI investigated this dangerous cartel leader and helped dismantle the criminal enterprise he allegedly used to poison American communities and fuel brutal violence. This arrest demonstrates the reach of HSI’s global investigative authorities and the strength of the HSTF as partners work together to take coordinated and relentless action against transnational criminal organizations that threaten our homeland.” Meza Flores is charged in a six-count superseding indictment filed in the District of Columbia with leading a continuing criminal enterprise, conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl for importation into the United States, international money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, and using a firearm including a machinegun and a destructive device. If convicted of these charges, Meza Flores faces the death penalty or a mandatory term of life in prison. The U.S. Department of State is offering a reward of up to $5 million for information that led to the arrest and/or will lead to the conviction of Chapo Isidro. If you have any information concerning Chapo Isidro, please contact your local FBI office or the nearest American Embassy or Consulate or call the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324). You can also submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov See: https://www.state.gov/fausto-isidro-meza-flores The HSTF including FBI Washington and San Diego Field Offices and HSI San Diego investigated the case with significant assistance from DEA, ATF, and the U.S. Marshals Service. Deputy Chief James Hepburn and Trial Attorney Jayce Born of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF) and Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua Mellor of the Southern District of California are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department's National Security Division, Office of International Affairs and Capital Case Section provided significant assistance. The Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section’s (MNF) mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations. MNF’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit investigates and prosecutes the top command and control elements of international drug cartels, drug trafficking organizations, and related transnational criminal organizations. This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. Updated November 21, 2026 Topic Homeland Security Task Force Component Office of the Attorney General Press Release Number: 26-1395

title: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
body:

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release November 20, 2026 Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955. Last Update:
            November 20, 2026

title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Corrupt Regime Insiders Exploiting Iran’s Oil Sector for Personal Gain
body: November 20, 2026 WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury is targeting key “oil trustees” the Iranian regime relies on to facilitate the sale of oil abroad. With no oil on the water outside of the U.S. military blockade and no oil loaded onto vessels since the start of Operation Economic Outcast, the regime is attempting to recoup billions of dollars from its oil trustees.  In many cases, these corrupt trustees have kept the oil revenue for personal gain. “Iran’s tyrannical regime never fails to put its own interests before those of its own citizens, even as ordinary Iranians face shortages of bread and fuel,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking.” The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy, and E.O. 13224, as amended, a counterterrorism authority. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day , Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime.  Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror.  Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast has significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. Operation Economic Outcast has also expanded sanctions exposure for non-U.S. persons who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . UNTRUSTWORTHY TRUSTEES Mohammad Javad Bavand (Bavand) and Majid Taj (Taj), the brother of the Iranian Football Federation’s president, operate as part of a network of regime insiders tasked with obtaining desperately needed cash by selling from Iran’s dwindling oil reserves.  Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence officer, has spearheaded this effort, entrusting a group of personal contacts, including Taj, to recoup Iran’s oil funds located in third countries.  The Iranian regime continues to entrust Bavand and Taj’s network with facilitating Iran’s oil sales, despite members owing billions of dollars to the regime from previous sales.  Bavand has worked with a variety of illicit oil trading actors, including the IRGC and Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company (SEJ), a U.S.-designated front company tasked with selling oil for the Iranian Armed Forces General Staff. Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. REGIME FACILITATORS Mohammadhossein Servati (Servati), the son of IRGC Brigadier General Mohsen Servati, has held executive positions at companies operated by SEJ, including SEJ front company Xin Rui Jin Trad Co., Limited , and Sepehr Energy Hamta Pars , a subsidiary of SEJ.  Xin Rui Jin Trad Co., Limited brokered and received shipments of Iranian oil on behalf of SEJ for delivery to Chinese teapot refineries. Mohammadhossein Servati is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company. Mojtaba Arabnejad (Mojtaba) is the son of the designated Iranian businessman and CEO of Iran’s Mahan Air , Hamid Arabnejad .  Using his familial ties and special connections with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF), Mojtaba has been involved in purchasing aircraft parts for Mahan Air and procuring weapons for the Iranian military under the auspices of agricultural companies.  Like others designated today, Mojtaba has overseen oil sales for the Iranian regime, the proceeds from which have supported Mahan Air. Mojtaba Arabnejad is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Mahan Air. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the United States or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000.  Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today.  This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List, when consistent with relevant statutes and other authorities.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is to bring about a positive change in behavior.  What constitutes a sufficient change in circumstance will vary based on context, including the status of the broader geopolitical circumstances affecting the national security and foreign policy interests implicated by the declared national emergency.  In the case of sanctions related to Iran, OFAC is employing all available statutory, regulatory, and policy tools to resolve the persistent national emergencies posed by Iran, which has not changed its behavior to align with U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives.  OFAC sanctions determinations, including removal determinations, are made consistent with Administration foreign policy and national security policies and priorities.  For more information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on How to Request Removal from an OFAC List. Click here for more information on today’s action. ###

title: Get your year-end tasks done with new Connected Apps.
body: Get your year-end tasks done with new Connected Apps. Nov 20, 2026 Tackling your to-do list just got a little easier. In the U.S., we’re rolling out new Connected Apps through Search and the Gemini app to help with your grocery runs, including Albertsons, Safeway, Shaw’s, and Target. Whether you’re preparing appetizers for your holiday party or need groceries for Thanksgiving, these new Connected Apps can help you build your order and check out with ease. Powered by the Universal Commerce Protocol , these apps can help you get more done this holiday season. The end of the year is also a great time to get your finances in order. Experian is already live on the Gemini app, and now we’re rolling it out to Search with the ability to help U.S. users check their credit rating and shop for a personal loan. U.S. users can also turn to H&R Block to calculate their taxes and estimate their refunds right from Search. In the coming weeks, you’ll also be able to link your accounts to Angi and Thumbtack in Search, streamlining your hunt for local pros who can fix that leaky faucet or put up last-minute decorations before your guests arrive.
retained_feed_body: Google Connected Apps simplify your year-end tasks. Manage groceries, credit scores, and home services directly in Search. Get the details for November 2026.

title: Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
body:
﻿ Speech by Governor Cook on the U.S. economy in global context - Federal Reserve Board Skip to main content An official website of the United States Government Here's how you know Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 20, 2026 The U.S. Economy in Global Context Governor Lisa D. Cook At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile Share Watch Live Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today. 1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking. I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic—to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently. Geopolitics and Trade Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated. A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy—that is not my role—but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room. The Global AI Buildout The third global force I want to highlight—and the one I will spend the most time on—is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world. While at the Board, I have spent much of my career as an economist studying innovation, including AI. Now, I spend considerable time talking with contacts in the U.S. and around the world about how AI is evolving and being used. I have spoken on several occasions about how I view AI—as a general-purpose technology, on par with or perhaps exceeding the steam engine, electrification, and the internet in its potential to transform how we work, innovate, and grow. This technology could bring a productivity boom unparalleled in generations. 2 At the same time, I worry deeply about our shared risks resulting from the technology, such as the specter of a painful labor market transition or cyber and financial-stability risks. Uncertainty abounds. In the U.S., AI has catalyzed a historic wave of investment. Companies have announced plans for more than $2 trillion in specific data center construction projects. So far, only a fraction of this has been realized. 3 This investment is already showing up in output data. And there is evidence of spillovers to other parts of the economy—in the price of chips and high-tech equipment, construction wages, and electricity costs. What I want to stress today is that this is not simply a North American phenomenon. By some estimates, roughly one-half of the world's data-center capacity now under construction is being built outside the U.S. 4 The AI buildout is a global undertaking, and it is reshaping economies—including economies in this region—in ways that are only beginning to be understood. Chile and its neighbors sit at an interesting intersection of this story. This country is the world's largest producer of copper and the second-largest producer of lithium—two minerals increasingly central to the infrastructure that AI requires, including power transmission and energy-storage systems. 5 This raises some questions to which I do not think any of us has a full answer. As demand for these minerals rises and falls with the pace of the global AI buildout, does this represent a new source of growth for resource-rich economies or a new source of volatility layered on top of already volatile commodity cycles? As capital flows toward AI infrastructure and related resource extraction around the world, what are the implications for smaller open economies managing capital flows, exchange rates, and financial stability? Corresponding to the buildout in physical infrastructure, adoption of AI tools by businesses and individuals is spreading quickly as well, albeit unevenly across countries. Recent work tracking the share of the working-age population using generative AI tools finds diffusion ranging from roughly 25 to 45 percent across higher-income economies, including Chile. These figures already exceed the pace of adoption we saw for personal computers at a comparable stage. 6 This matters a great deal for growth, because wider adoption of a general-purpose technology is ultimately how its productivity gains would be realized throughout an economy—gains that, in principle, could be sizeable. Simultaneously, researchers have raised questions about the distribution of gains across countries. Recent analysis from the International Monetary Fund suggests that advanced economies may be positioned to capture a disproportionate share of global AI-driven productivity growth over the next decade, relative to developing economies. 7 If this pattern holds, it raises important questions: Where in the distribution will countries like Chile wind up, and what might determine distributional outcomes? Finally, on the AI buildout, I would like to address AI and the labor market, the focus of today's conference. As with any major new technology, AI is likely to cause a shift in the labor market with jobs and job tasks being replaced by AI, and new jobs—many of which we cannot yet conceive of—being created. Ultimately, history has shown that human innovation will likely lead to a successful transition, with permanent job loss unlikely. However, I am very aware of the nonzero probability that this transition could take time and that job losses due to AI could precede new job creation. In the U.S., labor markets appear resilient to date, but AI adoption is still in its early stages, and I think it is too soon to feel comforted. We do see that some workers have already been affected by AI. For instance, there is already some evidence that labor demand has cooled for coding jobs in the software industry and in simultaneous translation. In addition, younger adults are experiencing prolonged job searches, which some attribute to nascent pressure from AI on entry-level positions. As AI adoption spreads, younger workers may continue to be disproportionately affected, and firms may need to take innovative and creative steps to train their future workforce. I am watching carefully the speed and acceleration of AI adoption across sectors and noting evidence of the changing mix of jobs within firms. New types of tasks and jobs are already being created, and I remain hopeful that job creation will be able to keep pace with job destruction. I will now turn to my outlook on the U.S. economy. U.S. Economic Outlook Overall economic growth in the U.S. is strong—and accelerating. The labor market remains solid, and, of great concern to me, inflation is well above the Fed's 2 percent target and has been for 67 months. I will start my forecast, as I typically do, with the price-stability side of our dual mandate, because, given the current state of the economy, this is my focus. Then, I will give my views on the path of monetary policy. One theme I want to emphasize is that waiting to act when a policy adjustment is required has a cost. Inflation Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, has exceeded the 2 percent target described in our framework for nearly six years. Based on U.S. inflation data released last week, it is estimated that the 12-month change in the PCE price index was 3.8 percent in October. The 12-month change in core prices—which exclude volatile food and energy costs—was 3.2 percent in October. The core measure underscores that, while energy is a significant contributor to inflation, the sources of price pressure facing American families are increasingly varied. Inflation soared in 2021 and 2022 because of supply disruptions and surging demand following the reopening of the U.S. and economies around the world as the global pandemic abated. The Fed, much like other central banks, responded by aggressively raising interest rates to fight inflation. I supported those actions as soon as I joined the Fed. From the middle of 2022 until the early part of last year, inflation moved down and appeared to be on a sustainable path back toward the 2 percent objective. However, a series of economic shocks over the past 18 months—including significant changes to trade policy, geopolitical developments, and massive investment in technological infrastructure—partially reversed that progress. Annual inflation in the U.S. has been steadily above 3 percent for much of this year, and, thus far, there is little evidence inflation is declining. In fact, the most recent inflation release showed that prices are rising briskly in a very broad range of categories—including airfare, appliances, furniture, hotels, and restaurants, to name a few. Labor market and output Next, I will turn to the labor market, the other half of the dual mandate assigned to the Fed by Congress. The U.S. labor market is solid, with still-low unemployment and consistent, though modest, hiring. The unemployment rate was 4.1 percent in October and has trended down modestly for nearly a year. As I have already mentioned, there is little evidence that AI is producing a significant imprint on the aggregate unemployment rate. Other data indicate the labor market is roughly in balance and gradually improving. Payrolls climbed by 165,000 in October, and some evidence is emerging that hiring is broadening to a wider array of sectors. Job openings in September were largely unchanged at 7.5 million, and initial unemployment claims, a proxy for layoffs, remain near historical lows—at a four-week moving average of about 195,000. Despite signs of strength, some Americans remain understandably frustrated with the state of the labor market. The "low hire" environment is particularly challenging for new entrants. And wages are growing but not enough to overcome the damaging effects of inflation. Still, low unemployment is consistent with achieving our maximum-employment mandate, and, therefore, as a monetary policymaker, I am more focused on the inflation side of our remit. Economic output in the U.S. has accelerated. GDP rose at a 3.4 percent annual pace in the third quarter, a pickup from already solid growth in the first half. The AI infrastructure buildout I previously discussed is a significant contributor to this acceleration. At the same time, American consumers have proven to be resilient, with real household spending rising an annualized 3.8 percent last quarter despite higher energy prices and broader inflationary pressure. Monetary Policy This leads to the path of U.S. monetary policy. The Federal Open Market Committee in September raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 3-3/4 to 4 percent to support a timelier return to the 2 percent objective. I supported that decision. At the most recent meeting, in October, the Committee voted to hold the policy rate steady. I dissented from that decision. I preferred to raise the target range another 1/4 percentage point. Two main reasons informed my decision to dissent. First, in my view, financial conditions are too accommodative at a time when inflation remains stubbornly above target, with no clear signs of disinflation in train. The current stance of policy does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout, and equity prices continue to support consumer spending. As a result, holding our policy rate steady will lead to a positive and widening output gap and increasing inflationary pressure. Indeed, we are seeing elevated inflation in a broad swath of goods and services. I see the act of holding the rate steady as much a monetary policy action as the act of increasing the rate. Second, my vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation. Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward. Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve. If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households. I have previously discussed my growing concern about the direction of inflation in several speeches this year. 8 I have called inflation unacceptably high. This remains my view. I have articulated my frustration that inflation has moved in the wrong direction as a series of shocks stacked upon each other. In addition, I noted that the extended time inflation had exceeded our target was an important part of my calculation. In a different environment, the Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury. I am skeptical that September's single 1/4 point rate increase will be enough to change the path of inflation. The number and magnitude of future adjustments should be informed by observations of the economy's reaction to our policy actions. The inflation data received since the September rate increase, including reports last week, fail to provide me with sufficient evidence that inflation is returning to a sustainable path. Conclusion Allow me to close where I began. The forces I have described today—geopolitical conflict, shifting trade relationships, and the buildout of AI—extend beyond national borders and weigh on the minds of monetary policymakers, including those in the U.S. and here in Chile. In terms of my view of U.S. policy, there is an overriding issue we must confront: Inflation has been above our target for far too long. I take great encouragement from the resilience of the labor market and the American economy—and the promise of the technologies now reshaping it. This promise will be best supported if we restore stable prices on which sustainable growth depends. Delivering on both sides of the dual mandate is the task before the Federal Reserve, and I am committed to seeing it through. Thank you for your time today, and thank you for the warm welcome back to Santiago. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text 2. See Lisa D. Cook (2026), " An Update on AI and the Economy ," speech delivered at Oakland Tech Week, cohosted by the Kapor Center, Oakland, California, September 28. Return to text 3. See Eirik Eylands Brandsaas, Daniel Garcia, Robert Kurtzman, Joseph Nichols, and Adelia Zytek (2025), "Estimating Aggregate Data Center Investment with Project-Level Data," Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2025-109 (Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, December), https://doi.org/10.17016/FEDS.2025.109 . For updated data, see Eirik Brandsaas (2026), DataCenterPublic, GitHub repository, https://github.com/eirikbrandsaas/DataCenterPublic. Return to text 4. Additional information is available on ABI Research's website at https://www.abiresearch.com/news-resources/chart-data/data-center-it-capacity-ai-workloads-forecast. Return to text 5. See National Minerals Information Center (2026), " 2024 Minerals Yearbook, volume III, Area Reports—International: Country Reports, Global Production, and Global Mineral Facilities ," U.S. Geological Survey Data Release, August 31. Return to text 6. See Sha Sajadieh, Loredana Fattorini, Raymond Perrault, Yolanda Gil, Vanessa Parli, Lapo Santarlasci, Juan Pava, Nestor Maslej, Russ Altman, Erik Brynjolfsson, Carla Brodley, Jack Clark, Virginia Dignum, Vipin Kumar, James Landay, Terah Lyons, James Manyika, Juan Carlos Niebles, Yoav Shoham, Elham Tabassi, Russell Wald, Toby Walsh, and Dan Weld (2026), The AI Index 2026 Annual Report (PDF) , AI Index Steering Committee, Institute for Human-Centered AI, Stanford University, April. Return to text 7. See Eugenio Cerutti, Antonio Garcia Pascual, Yosuke Kido, Longji Li, Giovanni Melina, Marina M. Tavares, and Philippe Wingender (2025), " The Global Impact of AI: Mind the Gap (PDF) ," IMF Working Paper No. 25/76 (Washington, D.C.: International Monetary Fund, April). Return to text 8. For example, see Lisa D. Cook (2026), " Economic Outlook ," speech delivered at the Economic Club of Miami, Miami, Florida, February 4; Lisa D. Cook (2026), " The Opportunities and Risks AI Presents for the Economy and Financial System ," speech delivered at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Stanford University, Stanford, California, May 27; Lisa D. Cook (2026), " Economic Outlook ," speech delivered at the Exchequer Club of Washington, D.C., Washington, July 15; Lisa D. Cook (2026), " Outlook for the U.S. and Alaskan Economies ," speech delivered at the 2026 Economic Luncheon of the Anchorage Economic Development Corporation, Anchorage, Alaska, August 5; and Cook, "An Update on AI and the Economy" (in note 2). In a February speech, I discussed my frustration that inflation appeared to have stalled stubbornly above our 2 percent goal. Based on the most recent data available at the time, I saw risks to our mandate tilting toward inflation and noted that the longer inflation remains above target, the greater the probability that higher inflation will become entrenched in expectations. I continue to be highly concerned about entrenched expectations. Similarly, in a speech in May, I mentioned that inflation was moving in the wrong direction. I said then that I was prepared to raise rates if disinflation did not appear in a timely manner. The data received in the six months since those remarks have shown no sign of such disinflation. In a July speech, I said that inflation was unacceptably high. That remains my view. And in an August speech I noted that the extended time inflation had exceeded our target was an important part of my calculus. In a late September speech, I expressed my support for the policy choice to raise rates because inflation had been too high for too long. Return to text Last Update:

title: How Watch Duty is using Gemini to get wildfire alerts out faster
body: How Watch Duty is using Gemini to get wildfire alerts out faster Nov 20, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Built with pro bono support from a Google.org Fellowship, a new Gemini-powered tool turns noisy fire radio into real-time text, helping Watch Duty spot new wildfire dispatches in under 30 seconds. Eve Andersson Senior Director for Social Impact Stephanie Chew Software Engineer Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X This July, as the Railroad Fire spread through Washington overnight, Watch Duty sent its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert to its users. It started with a 911 dispatch buried in radio static — and a new Gemini tool that caught it in seconds. A dedicated team of Google engineers and researchers spent six months embedded full-time with Watch Duty , a nonprofit wildfire alert app run by active and retired firefighters, dispatchers, and first responders. Through the Google.org Fellowship, they used more than 20,000 hours of past radio recordings to build a Gemini-powered tool that wipes out heavy static and translates specialized firefighting terminology into clean, searchable text. The system removes the added strain of deciphering noisy audio so volunteers can focus on verifying incidents and getting alerts out. The challenge When a wildfire starts, minutes can decide whether people get out safely. Yet across much of the country, the first word of a new fire still travels over decades-old analog VHF radio, where engine noise, wind, static, and rapid-fire tactical jargon make it hard to hear what's happening. Watch Duty reporters monitor up to 20 feeds manually, making it a challenge to cut through the noise. The results Across Watch Duty's network, the tool has: Helped close coverage gaps in areas with no other automated dispatch detection, sending reporters a signal in less than 30 seconds; this way, a new fire isn't missed just because no one was listening at that moment Reduced word error rate on degraded VHF radio audio from 38% down to 22.34% Transcribed more than 200 hours of radio speech a day from about 400 active feeds, and has been designed and tested to handle more than 10,000 feeds at once. As a result of the collaboration between Google and Watch Duty, volunteer reporter satisfaction with radio transcription tools increased from 35.3% to 92.3%. The tool was also put to test during a live fire. In July 2026, a fast-moving wildfire — the Railroad Fire — ignited at night in Washington. When the first 911 dispatch went out over local fire radio, the Gemini-powered transcription tool transcribed it straight from the noisy radio audio and flagged it in under 30 seconds. That head start gave Watch Duty's team the time they needed to verify the fire and push a Critical Alert—which breaks through do-not-disturb mode in urgent situations—helping residents evacuate before flames reached homes. It was the first time Watch Duty had ever sent a Critical Alert overnight, proving what faster detection means when communities are asleep and every minute counts. The collaboration The new AI radio tool is the latest milestone in a deep, multi-year collaboration spanning Google's philanthropic, product, and research teams to help Watch Duty scale its life-saving mission across all 50 states. Funding : In 2024, Google.org provided Watch Duty with $2 million in funding and $300,000 in Google Cloud credits to help compile satellite, camera, and radio data to validate new fires. Search : During US fires such as the Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, and Auto fires, Google Search featured Watch Duty in SOS alerts alongside official emergency guidance. Alerts at scale : Watch Duty sends push alerts through Firebase Cloud Messaging. As its audience grew to more than 16 million people last year, Google Cloud raised its messaging limit from 600,000 to 1 million to help alerts arrive without delay. Broader industry partnership : As part of the AI Collaborative: Wildfires , Watch Duty is turning models and data into tools that agencies, communities, and responders trust and use. When the next fire starts, the goal is simple: get people the warning they need while there's still time to act. ﻿ Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve Board releases results from survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances Skip to main content An official website of the United States Government Here's how you know Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.           the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial

Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release November 20, 2026 Federal Reserve Board releases results from survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances For release at 10:00 a.m. EST Share The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released results from a survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances. The Senior Financial Officer Survey is used by the Board to obtain information about banks' reserve balance management strategies and practices, their expectations around the size of their balance sheets and deposit balances their activity in money markets, and their views on other matters, such as operations on weekends and holidays. The survey was conducted in collaboration with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York between September 18, 2026, and September 28, 2026, and includes responses from banks that held around three-fourths of total banking system reserve balances at the time of the survey. For media inquiries, please e-mail [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955. Senior Financial Officer Survey (PDF) Last Update:
            November 20, 2026

title: Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises, 2024
body: News Release Explore Product View News Release Related Materials Contacts EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EST, Friday, November 20, 2026 BEA 26–49 Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises, 2024 Worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises increased 0.9 percent to 44.2 million workers in 2024 (preliminary) from 43.8 million workers in 2023 (revised), according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on the operations and finances of U.S. parent companies and their majority-owned foreign affiliates. Employment in the United States by U.S. parents increased 0.1 percent to 29.9 million workers in 2024. U.S. parents accounted for 67.6 percent of worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs), down from 68.1 percent in 2023. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates of U.S. MNEs increased 2.7 percent to 14.3 million workers and accounted for 32.4 percent of employment by U.S. MNEs worldwide. U.S. parents accounted for 21.7 percent of total private industry employment in the United States in 2024, down from 21.9 percent in 2023. Employment by U.S. parents was largest in manufacturing, in “other industries,” led by transportation and warehousing, and in retail trade. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates was largest in India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom. Worldwide current-dollar value added of U.S. MNEs increased 8.0 percent to $7.4 trillion in 2024. Value added by U.S. parents , a measure of U.S. parents’ direct contribution to U.S. gross domestic product, increased 8.5 percent to $5.7 trillion. U.S parents accounted for 21.8 percent of total U.S. private-industry value added, up from 21.2 percent in 2023. Foreign affiliate value added increased 6.5 percent to $1.8 trillion. Value added by foreign affiliates was largest in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada. Worldwide expenditures for property, plant, and equipment of U.S. MNEs increased 7.1 percent to $1.2 trillion. Expenditures by U.S. parents accounted for $968.7 billion, representing 36.5 percent of all U.S. private-business capital expenditures. Expenditures by foreign affiliates accounted for $216.2 billion. Worldwide research and development (R&D) expenditures of U.S. MNEs increased 10.1 percent to $622.7 billion. U.S. parents accounted for expenditures of $536.5 billion, representing 69.6 percent of business R&D performed in the United States. Foreign affiliates accounted for expenditures of $86.2 billion. Additional statistics on the activities of U.S. parent companies and their foreign affiliates , including sales, balance sheet and income statement items, compensation of employees, trade in goods, and more are available on BEA’s website. More industry detail for U.S. parents and more industry and country detail for foreign affiliates are also available on the website. Updates to the statistics Statistics for 2023 were revised to incorporate newly available and revised source data. Preliminary statistics for 2023 were released in August 2025. Updates to Statistics on 2023 Activities of U.S. Multinational Enterprises [Billions of dollars, except as noted] U.S. parents Majority-owned foreign affiliates Preliminary estimate Revised estimate Preliminary estimate Revised estimate Number of employees (thousands) 29,890.6 29,841.8 14,008.4 13,958.5 Value added 5,265.5 5,245.4 1,645.6 1,648.4 Expenditures for property, plant, and equipment 886.1 891.9 216.2 214.0 Research and development expenditures 476.6 481.5 81.7 84.1 U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis Related Data Tables For the 2024 activities of U.S. multinational enterprises statistics highlighted in this release, as well as estimates for earlier years, see the below data tables in BEA’s Interactive Data Application and comprehensive data tables . Selected data Selected Financial and Operating Data of U.S. Parents, by Industry of U.S. Parent Selected Data for Foreign Affiliates and U.S. Parents in All Industries Employment U.S. Parent Companies Employment, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates Employment, by Country Foreign Affiliates Employment, by Industry of Affiliate Foreign Affiliates Employment, by Country and Industry Value added U.S. Parent Companies Value Added, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates Value Added, by Country Foreign Affiliates Value Added, by Industry of Affiliate Expenditures for property, plant, and equipment (capital expenditures) U.S. Parent Companies Capital Expenditures, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates Capital Expenditures, by Country Foreign Affiliates Capital Expenditures, by Industry of Affiliate R&D expenditures U.S. Parent Companies R&D Expenditures, by Industry of U.S. Parent Company Foreign Affiliates R&D Expenditures, by Country Foreign Affiliates R&D Expenditures, by Industry of Affiliate Notes. This release includes, for the first time, statistics on U.S. parent shares of domestic activity for R&D performed and for property, plant, and equipment expenditures. BEA has updated its disclosure avoidance method to coarsening, which includes rounding, aggregation, and the use of ranges. This allows BEA to publish more data while still providing confidentiality to BEA’s survey respondents. For resources, definitions, statistical conventions, and more, visit " Additional Information ." Main Menu Toggle Button Sections Search Toggle Button Search Search Submit Button Submit Home News & Events Speeches Speech PDF November 20, 2026 Opening Remarks Governor Christopher J. Waller At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C. Share Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board. 1 We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University. Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy. A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals. Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions. Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools. In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade. I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge and developing research, analytical, and communication skills that will help you in whatever careers you choose. I'd like to thank the judges who have given their time and offered their expertise and experience to the evaluation of each team's work. They represent the very best of the Federal Reserve. From the Board we have Sriya Anbil, who is an economist in the Board's Division of Monetary Affairs; Karen Pence, who is a deputy director in the Division of Research and Statistics; and Brian Doyle, who is a deputy director in the Division of International Finance. And from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas we have Sam Schulhofer-Wohl, a senior vice president and senior adviser to president Lorie Logan. Also, let me again thank the faculty advisers of each of the seven teams for helping guide, motivate, and prepare today's finalists. And thanks also to the Federal Reserve's economic education staff who have organized the Fed Challenge this year and to all the judges who volunteered their time to make it possible. I am looking forward to a spirited competition, and I wish you all the best of luck. 1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. Return to text Last Update:

title: ADA Settlement Requires Accessibility Improvements at Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department
body: Press Release ADA Settlement Requires Accessibility Improvements at Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Middle District of Georgia Facility to Make Accessibility Improvements to Soccer Fields, Parking, and Restrooms MACON, Ga. – The Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department has agreed to make accessibility improvements across its facility following an investigation by the U.S. Attorney's Office into allegations that certain areas were not readily accessible to or usable by individuals with disabilities, as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). “We appreciate the cooperation shown by the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department in addressing these concerns and taking the necessary steps to improve accessibility,” said U.S. Attorney William R. “Will” Keyes. “When individuals and families raise concerns about barriers for people with disabilities, they help improve access for the entire community. The Americans with Disabilities Act plays a vital role in ensuring equal opportunity, and this agreement will help all members of the community fully access and enjoy the department's programs, services, and amenities.” The investigation was initiated by the U.S. Attorney’s Office after receiving a complaint from a family with multiple children with disabilities. The family frequently used the facility and services offered at 250 West Dykes Street, Cochran, Georgia, and reported that the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department did not provide adequate accessible parking; accessible restroom facilities; safe, stable walking surfaces to and from the restroom; and did not provide wheelchair access to several playing fields or any of the five soccer fields located within the 28-acre facility, all in violation of the ADA. Under the Letter of Resolution signed on Nov. 18, the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department has agreed to complete the following improvements: By Feb. 15, 2027, the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department will: Create the required number and type of designated accessible parking spaces; Construct an accessible restroom within the main concession building and install directional signage throughout the facility identifying its location; and Provide accessible routes connecting the soccer complex to the accessible restroom. By July 1, 2028, the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department will: Create an accessible route from the facility entrance through the soccer field complex, connecting to other athletic fields and the accessible restroom; and Create, improve, or repair accessible routes connecting facility entrances to playing fields, play areas, restrooms, and picnic shelters. Under federal law, discrimination based on disability in the services, facilities, privileges, advantages, or accommodations provided by entities such as the Cochran-Bleckley Recreation Department is prohibited. Public facilities are required to comply with the ADA's accessibility standards and must be readily accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities, including those who use wheelchairs and other mobility devices. ADA complaints may be made by contacting the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Georgia at (478) 752-3511. The investigation and resolution of this matter were led by Civil Rights Investigative Specialist Danyelle D. White, Civil Chief Bernard Snell, Assistant U.S. Attorney Hannah Couch, and former Assistant U.S. Attorney Lance Simon of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Georgia, in coordination with the Disability Rights Section of the U.S. Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division. Updated November 20, 2026 Topics Civil Rights Disability Rights Components Civil Rights Division USAO - Georgia, Middle

title: New Britain Man Admits Role in Firearms Trafficking Conspiracy
body: Press Release New Britain Man Admits Role in Firearms Trafficking Conspiracy Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Connecticut David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, and Thomas Greco, Special Agent in Charge, ATF Boston Field Division, today announced that DEMONTE HOLLEY, 38, of New Britain, pleaded guilty yesterday before U.S. District Judge Kari A. Dooley in Bridgeport to a firearms trafficking offense. As alleged in court documents and statements made in court, in September and October 2025, investigators arranged purchases of firearms from Jacintre Holley, who was incarcerated in federal prison and serving a sentence for trafficking firearms .  Jacintre Holley communicated with Demonte Holley, his cousin, to complete the transactions.  On October 1, 2025, Demonte Holley delivered a Glock pistol, equipped with a loaded high-capacity magazine, in exchange for $1,200.  On October 24, 2025, he delivered an Anderson Manufacturing AM-15 5.56 caliber pistol, a Palmetto State Armory Dagger Compact .9 mm pistol, and a Taurus International GX4 .9 mm pistol in exchange for $3,600.  The guns had been purchased in North Carolina, and Demonte Holley was told that the firearms being purchased were going to be sold in Maryland. On May 6, 2026, a grand jury in Bridgeport returned an indictment charging Jacintre Holley and Demonte Holley.  Demonte Holley was arrested on May 12, 2026.  Jacintre Holley died in custody in June 2026. Demonte Holley pleaded guilty to engaging in a firearms trafficking conspiracy, an offense that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of 15 years.  He is released on a $100,000 bond pending sentencing, which is scheduled, for February 11, 2027. As to Jacintre Holley, U.S. Attorney Sullivan stressed that an indictment is not evidence of guilt.  Charges are only allegations, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. This matter has been investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF).  The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Rahul Kale. Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Connecticut

title: Federal Jury Finds Couple Guilty of Wire Fraud and Money Laundering in Scheme to Defraud Medicare, Medicaid, and Private Insurers Out of Over $15 Million
body: Press Release Federal Jury Finds Couple Guilty of Wire Fraud and Money Laundering in Scheme to Defraud Medicare, Medicaid, and Private Insurers Out of Over $15 Million Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Minnesota ST. PAUL – United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen announced that a federal jury found two defendants guilty on all counts for their role in defrauding over $15 million in public funds. The guilty verdicts were returned on November 19, 2026, after an 11-day jury trial before Chief U.S. District Judge Eric C. Tostrud. Gabriel Adam Alexander Luthor, 40, and Elizabeth Christine Brown, 43, were each found guilty on seven counts, including six counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. They were indicted on March 6, 2025 , in the case United States v. Gabriel Luthor & Elizabeth Brown , No. 25-cr-88. Wire fraud is punishable by a maximum of 20 years in prison, and money laundering is punishable by a maximum of 10 years in prison. “The defendants took advantage of elderly patients and viewed them like an ATM, thinking they could just punch in the right codes, and money would come pouring out,” said United States Attorney Daniel N. Rosen. “I commend the work of our law enforcement partners who made this conviction possible. My office will continue to bring fraudsters like Luthor and Brown to justice.” According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Luthor and Brown used their neurofeedback-therapy company, Golden Victory Medical (GVM), to submit false medical bills to Medicare, Medicaid, and other health insurers. As part of the scheme, Luthor and Brown’s company billed for services that never occurred, billed for services performed by unlicensed technicians under the name of licensed professionals who did not actually perform the services, and billed for spending more time with patients than was true. For example, on 586 days, GVM falsely and impossibly claimed in its bills that its providers had spent more than 24 hours with patients. GVM’s providers—other than Elizabeth Brown—did not know what GVM was billing under their names. Graphic of the number of days that GVM claimed that its providers had provided over 24 hours of services Through the scheme, Luthor and Brown extracted more than $15 million from health insurers.  They used the fraud proceeds to dramatically increase their standard of living, buying luxury vehicles and a mansion in Eden Prairie, and spending large sums on luxury travel, to Vail and Miami, for example, and regular outings to nightclubs with bar tabs above $10,000. Luthor and Brown also laundered fraud proceeds, transferring approximately $350,000 through a series of bank accounts to fund a water-well drilling investment in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The scheme began in 2018, when Luthor and Brown—who were in a romantic relationship—were living in Las Vegas, Nevada. Brown had a master’s degree in nursing and a license to serve as an advanced practice registered nurse, commonly known as a nurse practitioner. Luthor had no medical training. In April 2018, Brown formed GVM, and shortly thereafter Luthor became a co-owner. Luthor and Brown’s scheme involved identifying potential patients, often elderly people who were confined to their homes or were in hospice care. The defendants then aggressively scheduled them for home visits by unlicensed neurofeedback “technicians” three times a week for neurofeedback sessions. Neurofeedback is an investigational or alternative medical service that is not covered by Medicare or virtually any private health insurer. For that reason, Luthor and Brown billed insurance for other services that were not neurofeedback, such as neurobehavioral and psychological examinations. The vast majority of these services did not occur, could not be performed by unlicensed and unsupervised technicians, and overrepresented the time spent with the patients. Luthor and Brown also did not have GVM charge the company’s patients copays, in violation of Medicare’s requirements. The lack of a copay led many of its largely elderly vulnerable patients to not notice or not take issue with the large amount GVM was billing to their insurance—though some patients noticed and complained. In 2019, Luthor and Brown moved to Minnesota where they purchased a million-dollar, 9,000-square-foot mansion in Eden Prairie. They funded the purchase with fraud proceeds and relocated GVM’s operational headquarters to the house. Luthor constantly pushed Brown to expand GVM’s footprint, resulting in GVM’s expansion beyond Las Vegas to additional clinics in Oklahoma, Kansas, and Florida. Photos of luxury property and vehicle purchased with fraud proceeds Luthor and Brown were warned repeatedly, year after year, about their false billing practices, but the defendants kept going. A doctor colleague of Brown’s complained about her billing practices to the Nevada and Minnesota boards of nursing. A nurse practitioner quit and complained that GVM was billing under her name for services she didn’t provide. A retired journalist complained that GVM was billing for services she had never received. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) suspended Medicare payments to GVM on suspicion of fraud. An outside auditor found that only 9% of GVM’s billing codes were supported. GVM’s CEO told Luthor and Brown that the billing problems, if left unfixed, could result in serious legal consequences—Luthor and Brown fired the CEO in retaliation. And an outside billing contractor also told Luthor and Brown they were billing too much for the services performed—Luthor and Brown fired the contractor. Despite all of these warnings, Luthor and Brown’s false billing practices continued. In early 2023, law enforcement executed search warrants at Luthor and Brown’s Eden Prairie residence and at GVM’s Las Vegas clinic. GVM then ceased doing business. This case is the result of an investigation conducted by the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Eden Prairie Police Department, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, and the U.S. Marshals Service. Assistant United States Attorneys Matthew D. Forbes and Matthew M. Paulbeck are prosecuting this case. Contact usamn.pressoffice@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Fraud Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Minnesota

title: District of Arizona Charges 314 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week
body: Press Release District of Arizona Charges 314 Individuals for Immigration-Related Criminal Conduct this Week Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona PHOENIX, Ariz. – During the week of enforcement operations from Nov. 14 through Nov. 20, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona brought immigration-related criminal charges against 314 individuals. Specifically, the United States filed 153 cases in which aliens illegally re-entered the United States, and the United States also charged 146 aliens for illegally entering the United States. In its ongoing effort to deter unlawful immigration, the United States filed 14 cases against 15 individuals responsible for smuggling illegal aliens into and within the District of Arizona. These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ICE-ERO), ICE- Homeland Security Investigations (ICE-HSI), U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). Recent matters of interest include: United States v. James Allen Lynch. James Allen Lynch was charged by criminal complaint on Nov. 17, 2026, with Transportation of an Illegal Alien for Profit. On Nov. 16, Border Patrol Agents (BPAs) observed at least two suspected illegal aliens cross the United States/Mexico border. Approximately five minutes later, agents observed a solo driver, Lynch, in a Chevrolet Blazer traveling southbound toward the same location. Lynch was in the area for approximately five minutes before he was observed driving away. Agents followed and saw multiple occupants in the back seat ducking out of view. Agents activated their emergency equipment to conduct an immigration inspection. Lynch continued at a slow pace before yielding a quarter mile later. As agents approached the vehicle, three subjects wearing camouflage attempted to exit but were stopped by agents. Agents searched the vehicle and apprehended two additional subjects in the trunk area. The five subjects were determined to be citizens of Mexico, illegally present in the United States. [Case Number: 26-MJ-12624] U.S. v. Jesus Romero-Morales . On Nov. 19, 2026, Jesus Romero-Morales was charged by criminal complaint with Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Nov. 18, a BPA in a marked vehicle was parked in the median of Interstate 40 (I-40) near Kingman, Arizona. The agent initiated an immigration inspection on Romero-Morales, who was driving a heavily tinted Ford Explorer. Inside the vehicle, the agent found five passengers, three of whom were citizens of China and two who were citizens of Mexico. All five were illegally present in the United States. The agent also learned that Romero-Rosales was a Mexican citizen without legal authority to be in the United States and that he had been paid to transport the aliens from Arizona to destinations in California. [Case Number: 26-MJ-01943] U.S. v. Carlos Yahir Moreno-Beltran. Carlos Yahir Moreno-Beltran was charged by criminal complaint on Nov. 19, 2026, for Transportation of an Illegal Alien. On Nov. 17, a BPA observed a Jeep Wrangler and a Dodge Ram truck driving in tandem northbound from a border construction area on South Avenue 25-East near Wellton, Arizona. The agent observed the vehicles separate at Old Highway 80, at which point the Jeep continued northbound before parking behind a barn. Upon seeing the BPA’s marked vehicle, multiple people were seen fleeing on foot from the Jeep. Another BPA located the Dodge Ram as it entered Interstate 8 heading eastbound. After the agent activated emergency lights to conduct an immigration stop, the driver of the truck, Moreno-Betran, accelerated and swerved on the roadway before crashing into another Border Patrol vehicle. Moreno-Beltran then led the BPA on a vehicle pursuit before agents used an immobilization device to bring him to a stop. Multiple occupants then fled from the truck. Additional agents responded to the area and ultimately apprehended 20 individuals. Emergency workers evaluated all 20 individuals for possible injury. Agents determined that four of the individuals were citizens of Mexico, four were citizens of Cuba, two were citizens of Colombia, one was a citizen of Ecuador, and one was a citizen of Guatemala. Agents further determined that all 20 individuals were illegally present in the United States. [Case Number 26-MJ-01942] A criminal complaint is a formal accusation of criminal conduct. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Contact Public Affairs Esther Winne Telephone: (602) 514-7740 Esther.Winne@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Arizona Press Release Number: 2026-191_November 20, 2026 Immigration Enforcement
