title: LOCAL OKANAGAN COUNTY DEPUTY HONORED NATIONALLY FOR HIS EXCEPTIONAL BRAVERY
body: Press Release LOCAL OKANAGAN COUNTY DEPUTY HONORED NATIONALLY FOR HIS EXCEPTIONAL BRAVERY Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Washington Spokane USAWAE.Media@usdoj.gov Spokane, Washington – First Assistant United States Attorney Pete Serrano announced that local Okanagan County Sergeant Kristopher Brakebill has been honored nationally for his exceptional bravery and heroism for his response in detaining multiple suspects involved in a violent murder spree that began on the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation. In October 2022, while investigating a separate homicide on the Colville Indian Reservation, Sergeant Kristopher Brakebill responded to reports of a robbery and double homicide in Keller, Washington. After spotting the suspects' vehicle, he initiated a solo pursuit through remote mountainous terrain. During the chase, suspects ambushed him multiple times, firing on his patrol vehicle and seriously wounding him. Despite being injured and without immediate backup, Sergeant Brakebill continued tracking the suspects, relaying critical information to responding officers until they were successfully intercepted and arrested. Serrano stated, “Sergeant Brakebill’s courage, determination, and commitment to public safety were instrumental in preventing the suspects' escape and bringing them to justice. I am honored to be able to sit alongside him as he received this award in Washington DC and thankful the Department recognized him along with every other brave and heroic law enforcement officer who responded that day.” Contact USAWAE.Media@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Component USAO - Washington, Eastern

title: Former Middle School Teacher Pleads Guilty to Money Laundering
body: Press Release Former Middle School Teacher Pleads Guilty to Money Laundering Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Texas WACO, Texas – A Waco man pleaded guilty in federal court for his scheme to launder more than $500,000 of stolen federal tax refunds, announced U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Texas, Justin R. Simmons. According to court documents, Jeremy Jarod Jackson pleaded guilty to one count of money laundering. In his plea, Jackson admitted to posing as a trustee of SWBC Professional Employee Services and changing the business address to direct tax refunds to himself. He obtained checks totaling $520,000, deposited the money into his accounts and spent it on personal items and services. Court documents also stated that an IRS Criminal Investigation special agent prevented Jackson from depositing more than $4 million in stolen refund checks into his accounts. Jackson, a former teacher at G. W. Carver Middle School in Waco, faces up to 10 years in prison on the money laundering charge. IRS-CI investigated the case with assistance from McLennan County Sheriff's Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Greg Gloff is prosecuting the case. ### Contact USATXW.MediaInquiry@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Tax Component USAO - Texas, Western

title: Federal Prosecutors Add More Than 560 Immigration Cases Through First Half of November in Western District of Texas
body: Press Release Federal Prosecutors Add More Than 560 Immigration Cases Through First Half of November in Western District of Texas Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Texas SAN ANTONIO – Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas filed 568 new immigration and immigration-related criminal cases from Nov. 6 through Nov. 20, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons. Charges were brought against alien smugglers and illegal aliens with past convictions for numerous DWIs, thefts, multiple prior removals, violent crimes, and sexual contact with children. Among the new cases, Adrian Duran Segura , an illegal alien from Mexico, was encountered in the Bexar County Jail after he was arrested for forgery and manufacture or delivery of a controlled substance. On Nov. 9, he pled guilty to three counts of indecency with a child by sexual contact and one count of indecency with a child by exposure. A Bexar County judge sentenced Duran, who was previously convicted in 1998 of criminal sexual conduct with a minor, to 10 years of deferred adjudication probation. Duran has been removed from the U.S. three times. Now in ICE custody, he faces another illegal re-entry charge. Also in San Antonio, Pedro Lara-Hernandez was arrested on Oct. 15 for assault of a family/household member. As an illegal alien from Mexico, he was turned over to ICE custody on Nov. 13 after being convicted of the assault charge and sentenced to five years of probation. Lara-Hernandez has multiple convictions in his criminal record, including attempted vehicle theft, evading arrest, evading arrest with a vehicle, and assault on a public servant. Two illegal aliens, each with five DWI convictions on their records, were charged with illegal re-entry in Austin. Juan Carlos Navarro-Espinoza , of Mexico, was found in the Travis County Jail on Nov. 3. Immigration records indicate he has been removed from the U.S. five times, the last being in 2019. Salvador Antonio Cruz Alvarado , of El Salvador, who was found in Bastrop County on Nov. 10. Cruz Alvarado, has also been deported five times, the last being in June 2020. Additionally, Cruz Alvarado was convicted in 2003 for evading arrest with a vehicle and in 2009 for possession of a controlled substance. Several more illegal aliens with multiple DWI convictions were also charged in Del Rio with illegal re-entry. Saul Avalos-Orona , an illegal alien from Mexico, was found near Knippa on Nov. 8, after being deported in January for the sixth time. Avalos-Orona has been convicted of DUI, driving while habitual violator, and DWI. Also an illegal alien from Mexico, Juan Gutierrez-Mejia was arrested on Nov. 7 near Brackettville. Gutierrez-Mejia was convicted of assault causing bodily injury in 2023 and, in 2025, was convicted of his third DWI. He was deported in June for the third time and is now charged with illegal re-entry. Eduardo Jurado-Resendiz , an illegal alien from Mexico, was found near Carrizo Springs on Nov. 5 after being deported in October. Jurado-Resendiz was convicted of DWI in December 2023, December 2024, and May 2026. Illegal alien from Mexico, Pedro Javier Vidal-Rios , was also found near Carrizo Springs this month. He was removed from the U.S. for the fifth time on Nov. 20, 2025, through Harlingen. Vidal-Rio has a lengthy criminal record that includes possession of a controlled substance, assault causing bodily injury, and at least three DWI convictions. Jonatan Galindo-Cardenas , an illegal alien from Honduras who has been deported seven times, was arrested near Knippa on Nov. 9. Galindo-Cardenas was most recently removed from the U.S. in June through Alexandria, Louisiana. His conviction record includes three illegal re-entries, one burglary and two convictions for grand theft auto. In El Paso, Belen Venegas-Rivera , an illegal alien from Mexico, was found on a bus that was going from the U.S. to Mexico through the Bridge of the Americas Port of Entry. A criminal complaint alleges Venegas-Rivera did not possess any legal documents and was in the U.S. illegally. Further inspection allegedly revealed Venegas-Rivera had crossed into the U.S. from Mexico near Aguas Prietas approximately 15 years ago. Records indicate he has been deported twice, and, in 2003, he was convicted of aggravated assault with a weapon. A U.S. citizen is charged in El Paso with alien smuggling. On Nov. 18, a U.S. Border Patrol agent near Fort Hancock pursued a vehicle suspected of picking up illegal aliens. The vehicle, driven by Jose Luis Cardenas , eventually came to a stop on westbound Interstate 10 near mile marker 82, according to a criminal complaint. Three individuals in the vehicle allegedly stated that they were citizens of Guatemala. A fourth passenger refused to answer but was later identified as an unaccompanied minor from Guatemala. Cardenas was arrested and charged. His extensive criminal record includes multiple trespass, burglary, and evading arrest convictions, as well as injury of a child/elderly/disabled with intent, taking from an officer, and possession of a controlled substance. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas comprises 68 counties located in the central and western areas of Texas, encompasses nearly 93,000 square miles and an estimated population of 7.6 million people. The district includes three of the five largest cities in Texas—San Antonio, Austin and El Paso—and shares 660 miles of common border with the Republic of Mexico. Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. These cases are part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. ### Contact USATXW.MediaInquiry@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Topics Operation Take Back America Human Smuggling Immigration Component USAO - Texas, Western

title: Illinois Man Charged with Possession and Transportation of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Illinois Man Charged with Possession and Transportation of Child Pornography Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Jersey An Illinois man was charged with possessing and transporting child sexual abuse material that had been generated using Super Intelligence (SI), U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced today. Donald Laycock, 47, of Joliet, Illinois, was charged by complaint with one count of possession of child pornography and one count of transportation of child pornography. Laycock made an initial appearance today before U.S. Magistrate Judge Young B. Kim in federal court in the Northern District of Illinois. According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court: In October 2026, law enforcement detained Laycock at Newark Liberty International Airport upon his return from an international trip. Law enforcement searched Laycock’s devices and located child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including CSAM that appeared to depict Laycock sexually assaulting minors. Laycock told law enforcement that he generated this and other CSAM using SI-enabled software and applications. “As alleged, the defendant used Super Intelligence to generate images and videos depicting grievous harm to children. SI’s image and video generation capabilities are advancing at an extraordinary pace. These charges highlight this Office’s dedication to protecting our children from the pernicious use of this rapidly evolving technology.” - U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer “The defendant is accused of creating, possessing, and transporting sexually explicit material involving children-conduct that inflicts lasting harm on victims and threatens the safety of communities everywhere,” said Special Agent in Charge Michael S. McCarthy. “One victim is one too many, and behind every child exploitation investigation is a child whose innocence has been violated. HSI New Jersey remains steadfast in its commitment to protecting vulnerable members of our communities and holding accountable those who seek to harm them.” As charged, each of the possession and transportation of child pornography charges carry a maximum penalty of twenty years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of transportation of child pornography also carries a mandatory minimum sentence of five years. U.S. Attorney Frazer credited the work of Homeland Security Investigations New Jersey, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Michael S. McCarthy, with the investigation leading to the charges. U.S. Attorney Frazer also thanked Homeland Security Investigations Chicago, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Matthew Scarpino, and the Will County, Illinois Sheriff’s Office for their assistance. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) in the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit: https://www.justice.gov/psc . U.S. Attorney Frazer has announced proactive steps to connect with New Jersey’s families and communities, bringing training opportunities and resources through direct outreach. Organizations and community members interested in arranging prevention programming or learning more about available resources can contact the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey at USANJ.CommunityOutreach@usdoj.gov . Moreover, prevention resources are available through the Department of Justice's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section Prevention webpage and the Department of Homeland Security’s Know2Protect Campaign. The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorney Dylan P. McGowan of the General Crimes Unit in Newark. The charges and allegations contained in the complaint are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. ### Defense counsel: Philip R. Nathe, Esq. laycock.complaint.pdf ^ On September 29, 2026, President Donald J. Trump issued Executive Order No. 14434, which declared that the terms “Super Intelligence” or “SI” more appropriately describe those technologies widely known as “Artificial Intelligence” or “AI.” See Exec. Order 14434, 91 Fed. Reg. 63129 (Sep. 29, 2026). Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - New Jersey Press Release Number: 26-260

title: Former L.A. Resident Found Guilty of Federal Charges for Deliberately Starting What Became the Palisades Fire Last Year
body: Press Release Former L.A. Resident Found Guilty of Federal Charges for Deliberately Starting What Became the Palisades Fire Last Year Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California LOS ANGELES – A former Los Angeles resident was found guilty by a jury today of starting what became the Palisades Fire of January 2025, the most destructive wildfire in the city’s history. Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, a.k.a. “Jonathan Rinder,” and “Jon Rinder,” was found guilty of one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. “Twelve people lost their lives and thousands lost their homes because of Jonathan Rinderknecht’s malicious conduct,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the persistence and hard work of our prosecutors in the Central District of California, he will be held accountable.” “Jonathan Rinderknecht deliberately ignited a fire that killed 12 people and devastated an entire community,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.” According to evidence presented at a 14-day trial, on January 1, 2025, Rinderknecht ignited what came to be known as the Lachman and Palisades fires. In the days leading up to the Lachman Fire, Rinderknecht exhibited extreme anger, indignation, and frustration about being unable to find companionship on New Year’s Eve 2024 and about a former co-worker whom he briefly dated in March 2024. Alone on New Year’s Eve, Rinderknecht drove several Uber passengers, nearly all of whom remembered him being angry that night. He dropped off his final Uber passenger in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles and drove to The Summit, a neighborhood where he had lived a few years earlier with a former lover. Rinderknecht drove towards Skull Rock Trailhead, parked his car, attempted to contact a former friend, and walked up the trail. He then used his iPhone to take videos at a nearby hilltop area and listened to a rap song – to which he had listened repeatedly in previous days – whose music video included things being lit on fire. When Rinderknecht maliciously started the Lachman Fire just after midnight, he was alone in a small clearing on Hidden Buddha Hill in Pacific Palisades. At approximately 12:12 a.m. on January 1, 2025, environmental sensing platforms indicated the Lachman Fire had begun. During the next five minutes, Rinderknecht called 911 several times, but didn’t get through because his iPhone was out of cellphone range. When he finally connected with 911, he was at the bottom of the hiking trail and reported the fire. By that point, a nearby resident already had reported the fire to authorities. Rinderknecht then fled in his car, passing fire engines driving in the opposite direction. He then turned around and followed the fire engines to the scene, driving at a high rate of speed. Rinderknecht walked up the same trail from earlier that night to watch the fire and the firefighters. At approximately 1:02 a.m., he used his iPhone to take more videos of the scene. During an interview with law enforcement on January 24, 2025, Rinderknecht lied about where he was when he first saw the Lachman Fire. He claimed he was near the bottom of a hiking trail when he first saw the fire and called 911, but geolocation data from his iPhone carrier showed that he was standing in a clearing 30 feet from the fire as it rapidly grew. Although firefighters quickly suppressed the Lachman Fire, the fire continued to smolder and burn underground within the root structure of dense vegetation. On January 7, 2025, heavy winds caused the underground fire to surface and spread above ground in what became known as the Palisades Fire, which caused widespread damage in Pacific Palisades, killing 12 people, and destroyed 6,837 structures, causing an estimated $25 billion in damage in the most destructive wildfire in the city’s history. United States District Judge Anne Hwang scheduled a March 17, 2027 sentencing hearing, at which time Rinderknecht would face a mandatory minimum sentence of five years in federal prison and a statutory maximum sentence of 40 years in federal prison. Rinderknecht has been in federal custody since October 2025. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is investigating this matter with substantial assistance from the Los Angeles Police Department and the United States Forest Service. Assistant United States Attorneys Mark A. Williams, Matthew W. O’Brien, and Danbee C. Kim of the Environmental Crimes and Consumer Protection Section are prosecuting this case. If you are a victim of the Palisades Fire, updates about this criminal case can be found on this webpage . Contact Shawn Lewis Public Affairs Officer shawn.lewis@usdoj.gov (213) 458-6803 Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - California, Central Press Release Number: 26-224
retained_feed_body: A former Los Angeles resident was found guilty by a jury today of starting what became the Palisades Fire of January 2025, the most destructive wildfire in the city’s history.

title: Illegal alien charged with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship at DFW Airport
body: Press Release Illegal alien charged with falsely claiming U.S. citizenship at DFW Airport Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Texas Defendant entered the county dozens of times with fraudulently obtained U.S. passport FORT WORTH, Texas — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced that an illegal alien from Mexico has been indicted for falsely claiming to be a U.S. Citizen after allegedly attempting to enter the country using a fraudulently obtained U.S. passport at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. On Nov. 18, a grand jury returned a two-count indictment charging Francisco Federico Reyes-Bravo, 45, for falsely and willfully claiming to be a U.S. citizen and misuse of a passport. “Falsely claiming U.S. citizenship is not a paperwork violation; it is a serious federal offense that threatens our national security and undermines the integrity of our immigration system,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “According to the allegations, the defendant repeatedly relied on a fraudulently obtained U.S. passport and another person's identity to evade lawful scrutiny to illegally enter the United States. My office will aggressively pursue anyone who circumvents U.S. law and compromises the security measures that protect the American people.” According to the criminal complaint, on Oct. 28, Reyes-Bravo arrived at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport aboard a flight from Veracruz, Mexico. He allegedly presented a United States passport bearing the name Javier Torres Rodriguez and claimed to be a U.S. citizen while seeking admission into the United States. The complaint alleges that during a secondary inspection conducted by U.S Customs and Border Protection officers, fingerprint analysis determined that the defendant was not a U.S. Citizen, but a Mexican national identified as Francisco Federico Reyes-Bravo with an active warrant issued by the Riverside County Sheriff’s Department in California. After being advised of his rights, the defendant admitted he was born in Ensenada, Baja California, Mexico. According to court documents, investigators determined that the U.S. passport presented by the defendant had been used to enter the United States 42 times through air and land ports of entry between 2018 and 2026. The complaint further alleges that the passport was obtained through the submission of fraudulent identity and citizenship documents, including a birth certificate and driver's license belonging to another individual. Reyes-Bravo is currently in federal custody. If convicted, the defendant faces a prison term of up to three years in federal prison for fraudulently claiming to be a U.S. Citizen and up to 10 years for misuse of a passport. U.S. Customs and Border Protection investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Connor Day from the Fort Worth Division is prosecuting the case. An indictment is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law. . ### Documents francisco_reyes_bravo_indictment.pdf reyes_bravo_complaint.pdf Contact Public Affairs Division U.S. Attorney’s Office Northern District of Texas USATXN.Media@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Texas, Northern

title: Hartford Man Sentenced to 6 Years in Federal Prison for Illegal Gun Possession
body: Press Release Hartford Man Sentenced to 6 Years in Federal Prison for Illegal Gun Possession Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Connecticut David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced that LAWRENCE SMALL, 33, of Hartford, was sentenced today by U.S. District Judge Kari A. Dooley in Bridgeport to 72 months of imprisonment and three years of supervised release for unlawfully possessing a firearm. According to court documents and statements made court, a state parole officer notified Hartford Police of an arrest warrant for Small, who had absconded from special parole.  In the early morning of March 30, 2025, Hartford Police identified Small as he left an apartment on Wethersfield Avenue and entered his car.  Small was forcibly removed from the car after he ignored officers’ demands.  A subsequent search of the vehicle revealed a loaded firearm with an extended magazine. Small’s criminal history includes felony convictions for robbery, assault, firearm, and escape offenses.  It is a violation of federal law for a person previously convicted of a felony offense to possess a firearm or ammunition that has moved in interstate or foreign commerce. Small has been detained since his arrest.  On July 31, 2026, he pleaded guilty to unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon. This matter was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Hartford Police Department.  The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney John T. Pierpont, Jr. Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Connecticut

title: Federal grand jury indicts Albion man for defrauding the VA out of hundreds of thousands of dollars
body: Press Release Federal grand jury indicts Albion man for defrauding the VA out of hundreds of thousands of dollars Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of New York BUFFALO, N.Y. - U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that a federal grand jury has returned an indictment charging Timmie L. Haynes, 64, of Albion, NY, with five counts of wire fraud, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. This action is part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. According to the indictment, Haynes served in the U.S. Army between December 4, 1979, and October 21, 1980, when he received a General Discharge Under Honorable Conditions. Shortly after being discharged, Haynes applied for Veterans Affairs (VA) disability benefits, which are monthly payments based on the severity of the disability rating, ranging from 0% (no compensation) to 100% (maximum compensation). Haynes claimed arthritis in his hand, wrist, knee joints, and lower back and was granted service-connected disability, but at a 0% compensation rating effective October 22, 1980. Haynes repeatedly sought increased compensation ratings, claiming progressively worsening joint conditions, eventually receiving a 100% rating effective October 31, 1989. Between 1991 and 1994, Haynes falsely claimed to the VA that he was wheelchair bound and presented himself as virtually immobile from the waist down. As a result of these false representations, on February 10, 1995, the VA granted Haynes Special Monthly Compensation (SMC), for loss of use of both of his legs. SMC is an additional benefit for veterans with severe service-connected disabilities. In addition, between 2004 and 2026, Haynes applied for and received funds from the VA’s Automobile Allowance and Special Adaptive Equipment Program, the Home Improvements and Structural Alterations Program, and the Veteran-Directed Care, to help with activities of daily living. During this time, Haynes also fought attempts to reduce his monthly benefit payment and discontinuance of his SMC after the VA received information that he no longer met the criteria to receive the benefit. In furtherance of his scheme to defraud, Haynes falsely represented to the VA that he was wheelchair bound, unable to walk, unable to use his left hand, and that he needed assistance with activities of daily living. In truth, from 1989 to the present, Haynes was not wheelchair bound and did not lack the use of his legs or left hand. Haynes could walk unassisted, drive without adaptive equipment, lift and carry objects, shop in stores without assistance, and perform other physical activities. As a result of his false representations, between 1989 and the present, Haynes received compensation and benefits totaling approximately $1,024,884.90. Haynes was arraigned before U.S. Magistrate Judge Jeremiah J. McCarthy and was released on conditions. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul E. Bonanno and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Crystal R. Willis. The indictment is the result of an investigation by the Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Inspector, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Christopher F. Algieri, Northeast Field Office and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis, II. The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty. # # # # Contact Barbara Burns 716-843-5817 Updated November 20, 2026 Topics Fraud Benefit Fraud Financial Fraud Component USAO - New York, Western

title: Cheyenne Resident Charged with Wire Fraud and Money Laundering in Connection with $270,000 Fraud Scheme
body: Press Release Cheyenne Resident Charged with Wire Fraud and Money Laundering in Connection with $270,000 Fraud Scheme Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Wyoming usawy.pio@usdoj.gov CHEYENNE, Wyo. – A federal indictment has been unsealed charging Ariyan Devonte Trawick , of Cheyenne, in connection with a scheme to defraud three victims between March and August 2024. According to the indictment, Trawick is alleged to have used Wyoming registered business entities to open accounts at two financial institutions in Cheyenne to receive and launder illicit funds. It is further alleged that in June of 2024, three victims were fraudulently induced into wiring a total of $270,000 into an account controlled by the defendant. The indictment further alleges that Trawick transferred, or attempted to transfer, the proceeds of the fraud to domestic and international beneficiaries, including recipients in California and Hong Kong. Trawick is charged with four counts of wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, as well as three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in property derived from specified unlawful activity, commonly referred to as money laundering. U.S. Attorney for the District of Wyoming Darin D. Smith announced the charges following an investigation by IRS Criminal Investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Margaret Vierbuchen is prosecuting the case. A jury trial is scheduled for January 4, 2027, at 1:30 p.m. before U.S. District Court Judge Alan B. Johnson. An indictment is merely an allegation, and the defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ### Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Fraud Components Criminal - Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section Cyber Division (FBI) National Fraud Enforcement Division USAO - Wyoming Press Release Number: 26-057

title: Nigerian Man Sentenced to 24 Months for Aggravated Identity Theft
body: Press Release Nigerian Man Sentenced to 24 Months for Aggravated Identity Theft Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nebraska United States Attorney Lesley A. Woods announced that Chukwuebuka Madueke Arinze, 38, of Nigeria, was sentenced on October 30, 2026, in federal court in Omaha, Nebraska, for aggravated identity theft. United States District Judge Robert F. Rossiter, Jr. sentenced Arinze to 24 months’ imprisonment. There is no parole in the federal system. After Arinze’s release from prison, he will begin a one-year term of supervised release. Arinze will be removed from the United States once he completes his sentence. The Coronavirus Food Assistance Program (CFAP) is a financial assistance program through the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) that was created in response to the COVID-19 Pandemic. CFAP is administered through the USDA's Farm Service Agency (FSA) and Agricultural Marking Service (AMS). The purpose of CFAP was to provide financial assistance to producers of agricultural commodities with financial assistance that would assist them in absorbing losses in sales and increased marketing costs due to the COVID-19 pandemic. CFAP was funded through the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Stability Act (CARES Act) and the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC) Charter Act. Agricultural producers who were eligible must have suffered a five percent or-greater price decline as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic and face substantial marketing costs for inventories. The producers must also be engaged in the production of specified agricultural commodities to include certain specialty crops, non-specialty crops, wool, dairy, aquaculture, nursery crops and cut flowers, eggs, and livestock. CFAP applications were accepted from May 26, 2020, through September 11, 2020. The USDA extended a second round of assistance beginning on September 21, 2020, in what was known as CFAP2. The FSA accepted the CFAP2 applications from September 21, 2020, through December 11, 2020. CF AP and CFAP2 were self-certification programs. As such, producers did not need to provide documentation of pandemic-related losses to their operations in order to apply. On or about September 28, 2020, Arinze, while residing outside of the United States, sent an email with the subject line "CFAP Forms" which contained a CFAP2 application and ACH form in the name of Victim 1 (a dairy producer residing in Wayne, Nebraska) to FSA Office in Wayne, Nebraska. The CFAP2 application contained Victim 1’s Social Security Number and was used as a method to validate the legitimacy of the application. Arinze knew that this Social Security Number was assigned to Victim 1. He also knew that he was using this Social Security Number without lawful authority. Arinze was brought to the United States to face charges. On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Contact Amy Donato 402-661-3700 Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Fraud Components National Fraud Enforcement Division USAO - Nebraska

title: Albuquerque Man Charged with Diverting Estate Funds for Personal Use
body: Press Release Albuquerque Man Charged with Diverting Estate Funds for Personal Use Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Mexico ALBUQUERQUE – An Albuquerque man already facing federal fraud, money laundering, and tax charges in a separate case has been indicted for allegedly transferring estate and trust funds into accounts under his control and using the proceeds for his personal benefit. According to court records, from March 2023 to April 2023, James Joseph Owens , 68, while serving as the personal representative of the estate of a deceased Albuquerque resident and as trustee of the family's revocable trust, allegedly abused his position of trust by misappropriating estate and trust assets for his personal benefit. Prosecutors allege that after receiving a $171,561.12 death benefit payment intended for the Family Revocable Trust and its beneficiaries, Owens transferred $151,000 from trust accounts into bank accounts he personally controlled. Owens also allegedly used funds derived from the scheme to purchase cryptocurrency and concealed certain financial accounts and transactions from the probate court. The case marks the second federal fraud indictment filed against Owens in 2026. In a separate pending case , prosecutors accuse him of embezzling more than $2 million from the Norbertine Community of New Mexico while serving as the religious community's treasurer. Federal prosecutors argued in court filings that both cases involve a similar pattern of gaining positions of trust and then exploiting those positions for personal financial gain. Owens is federally charged with one count of wire fraud and two counts of engaging in monetary transactions in property derived from unlawful activity. If convicted of these new charges, Owens faces up to 20 years in prison. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Acting Special Agent in Charge Scott Brown of IRS Criminal Investigation's Phoenix Field Office, made the announcement today. IRS Criminal Investigation investigated this case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Sean J. Sullivan and Fredrick T. Mendenhall are prosecuting the case. An indictment or criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Financial Fraud Component USAO - New Mexico Press Release Number: 26-325

title: Attorney General Blanche Honors Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry for Distinguished Service
body: Press Release Attorney General Blanche Honors Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry for Distinguished Service Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Arizona WASHINGTON – Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry was among the law enforcement officers from around the nation who were selected to be honored by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche today for Distinguished Service in Policing. This award represents the Department of Justice’s reaffirmed commitment to uplifting the valor and exceptional contributions to policing of our great nation’s law enforcement personnel. The Attorney General’s Honor the Honorable Award recognizes officers from state, local, Tribal or territorial law enforcement agencies for exceptional efforts in policing. The awarded officers, deputies, and troopers have demonstrated exceptional service in one of three areas: criminal investigations, field operations or exemplary community involvement. Within each category, awards were given to law enforcement officers and deputies who serve small, medium and large jurisdictions. Officer Berry was among the officers selected for the field operations category, which is intended to award those who have demonstrated exceptional bravery; heroic, quick, innovative, or otherwise exceptional problem-solving; and sustained excellence in achieving law enforcement goals, engaging in direct action to preserve life, or making a significant arrest. The Department of Justice award states, “In the early morning hours of May 25, 2025, Goodyear Police Officer Dakota Berry was returning to the city after completing a suspect booking when he encountered a catastrophic multivehicle collision. One vehicle was fully engulfed in flames. Trapped inside the burning car was a lone driver, frantically sounding the horn in a desperate plea for help. Without regard for his own safety, Officer Berry acted decisively and heroically. He broke the driver’s side window, reached into the inferno, and pulled the driver—whose hair was on fire—from the engulfed vehicle. Realizing the flames on the driver’s body were still active, Officer Berry immediately used his bare hands to extinguish the fire, sustaining significant burn injuries. After suppressing the flames on the victim, he located and used a fire extinguisher to eliminate the remaining fire on her person.” The award continues, “Thanks to his courageous actions, the victim—later identified as the daughter of a Goodyear firefighter—was transported in critical condition to a burn center, where she survived and continues to recover. Officer Berry also received treatment at a local burn center and made a full recovery from his injuries. The incident was captured in graphic detail by Officer Berry’s body-worn camera, drawing national attention and praise. Officer Berry’s quick thinking, fearless intervention, and unwavering dedication to duty unquestionably saved the woman’s life. His selfless courage, even in the face of immediate and life-threatening danger, reflects the highest ideals of policing and public service.” “Officer Berry represents the best of the best in bravery, selfless service, and community devotion,” said U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine. “Putting aside any thought for his own safety, Officer Berry ran toward danger to save a life. We are honored to have him serving here in Arizona.” “I was honored to recognize the very best of local law enforcement at the Department of Justice today,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These men and women are playing a critical role in our effort to Make America Safe Again. The Trump Administration will never apologize for backing the blue and supporting local law enforcement.” “I am constantly mindful that even with all the resources available at the Department of Justice, it is local law enforcement who are on the front lines of making our country safe again,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward.  “The leadership of this Department of Justice never misses an opportunity to thank them for that.” The awardees for all categories were selected from a nationwide pool of nominees for their outstanding achievements and commitment to making American safe again. Nominations are now being accepted for next year’s ceremony and nomination information can be found here . More information about the awards can be found online: https://www.justice.gov/ag/policing-award RELEASE NUMBER:    2026-192_COPS Awards # # # For more information on the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Arizona, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao/az/ Follow the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Arizona, on Twitter @USAO_AZ for the latest news. Contact Public Affairs Esther J. Winne Telephone: (602) 514-7740 Esther.Winne@usdoj.gov Updated November 20, 2026 Component USAO - Arizona Press Release Number: 2026-192_COPS Awards

title: Snapchat User Sentenced to 16 Years in Prison for Receiving Child Sexual Abuse Material
body: Press Release Snapchat User Sentenced to 16 Years in Prison for Receiving Child Sexual Abuse Material Friday, November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of North Carolina ASHEVILLE, N.C. – James Noah Hughes, 22, of Otto, North Carolina, was sentenced to 192 months in prison yesterday for receiving child sexual abuse material (CSAM), announced Russ Ferguson, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of North Carolina. Hughes was also ordered to serve a lifetime of supervised release and to register as a sex offender. According to filed court documents and the sentencing hearing, in 2024, Hughes used Snapchat to communicate with a minor female and to request sexually explicit images and videos from the minor. Hughes would also photograph himself and the minor engaged in sexually explicit conduct. Court records show that Hughes would then use the images and videos to threaten the minor that he would expose her to her family unless she created and sent him sexually explicit images and videos of herself. Court records show Hughes also threatened to physically harm himself and the minor if she did not continue to comply with his demands. Hughes was found in possession of over 7,000 images containing child sexual abuse material depicting the minor female victim and other identified and unidentified victims. Hughes remains in federal custody until he is transferred to the custody of the Federal Bureau of Prisons upon designation of a federal facility. In making the announcement U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson commended HSI and the Macon County Sheriff’s Office for their work on this case. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Asheville prosecuted the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . Updated November 20, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - North Carolina, Western

title: Combatting adversarial distillation
body: November 20, 2026 Combatting adversarial distillation How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry. Share As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked. We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry. Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity. We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards. Why distillation is a safety issue Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why . Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them. The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked. The importance of protecting exact reasoning traces for cyber safety Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities. In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces. We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. 1 Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies . Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes. Defenses that reinforce one another We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards. Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards. Protecting individual requests and responses D efensive training for model behavior Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners. Classifier safeguards We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses. Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller. API-level protections API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning. Investigating and disrupting coordinated campaigns When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services. This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments. S haring relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models . Measuring progress Resistance to reasoning extraction To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss. We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well. Attack type GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards Adaptive extraction ASR (%) GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards Adaptive extraction ASR (%) Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request 54.0 0.2 Extracting protected reasoning from the current request 22.9 0.9 Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better. Campaign detection and enforcement We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report . Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer. In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, w e also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations. The national security implications of adversarial distillation Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed ⁠ (opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted. We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards. How others can build on this work Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take: Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models. Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses. Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement. Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry. We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum ⁠ (opens in a new window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private . We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses. As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity. Footnotes 1 Related work from Anthropic ⁠ (opens in a new window) reported a similar advantage when training on full reasoning transcripts rather than summaries on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering benchmark. Our result shows this advantage extends to frontier cybersecurity. title: Christine Lagarde: Acting in time
body:
Acting in time Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Christine Lagarde The President of the European Central Bank SPEECH Acting in time Keynote speech by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress Frankfurt am Main, 20 November 2026 It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last. In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market. But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere. For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding. Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right. The old challenges and the new ones have something in common. Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”. Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed. Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing. Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way. Why Europe acts in some crises but not others It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome. My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others. When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another. Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion. Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO. Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing. What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back. Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is certain and has to be paid straight away. Both the old challenges and the new ones are of this kind. Take capital markets. We have all agreed for more than a decade that Europe needs a capital markets union. But building it means taking on vested interests now, for gains that arrive years later. Each year without it, more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding. Yet no single year’s loss is large enough to overcome the resistance to change. We have seen this again in recent weeks. The Council has just agreed its position on strengthening the supervision of capital markets, which is welcome. But the position weakens the European supervisor’s ability to take effective decisions and includes too many carve-outs. Our dependencies raise the same problem. Reducing them means paying for new capacity now, against a threat that may never materialise. One recent estimate suggests that raising Europe’s share of the world’s AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030 would require investment of around €1.3 trillion. [ 1 ] But as long as we can buy computing power from foreign providers and frontier AI models remain available to us, the case for paying that price is hard to make. In both, the cost of inaction is real, whether it is a loss we are already suffering or a danger we may face tomorrow. But it rarely becomes visible enough to build the broad consensus for change that we found for the pandemic or for Ukraine. This is the central problem of European policymaking. We can see the problem early, but we can act only once it has become impossible to ignore. And by then, almost by definition, it is too late. Lost industries are very hard to win back, and once a dependency has been used against us, our sovereignty is already exposed. Think of the euro area debt crisis. The scale of Greece’s difficulties was clear long before Europe acted decisively to strengthen its institutions. We paid a much higher price than if we had acted earlier, including a six-quarter recession. We often hear that policymakers in Europe do not understand the problems they face. I think they do. The difficulty is that they are asked to impose visible costs on their citizens today, for benefits that will only become apparent over time, before a majority is convinced that action is needed. These are among the hardest decisions in public life, and I have a great deal of sympathy for those who have to take them. At the ECB, we have had to take some of them too. Acting early at the ECB Economic sovereignty is not an objective in itself for us. Our primary objective is price stability, and the Treaty also gives us the tasks of issuing money and promoting the smooth operation of payment systems. But a changing world bears directly on those tasks, and during my term it has confronted us with slow-moving risks of our own. We have faced decisions of this kind in three areas. In each, we had to choose whether to invest early in something whose value would only become clear later. The first area was retail payments. Since the euro was introduced, Europeans have had a single means of payment that works everywhere in the euro area: euro cash. But for card payments, we have relied on providers from outside Europe. International card schemes handle more than 60% of our card payments, and 14 of the 21 euro area countries have no domestic scheme at all. [ 2 ] For a long time, this did not seem to matter, because cash was still the dominant means of payment. The international schemes worked well, and no one had ever cut Europe off. The private sector tried more than once to build a European alternative, but each attempt ran into the same vicious circle: merchants will not adopt a scheme that few customers use, and customers will not use one that few merchants accept. But cash is playing a smaller role as more of our spending moves online, where more than a third of our day-to-day spending now takes place. [ 3 ] And the geopolitical climate has changed. We have already seen judges of the International Criminal Court living in Europe, some of them European citizens, lose the use of their bank cards overnight. So we concluded that Europe needed a digital equivalent of cash: the digital euro. It will give Europeans a means of payment that runs on European infrastructure. And as legal tender, it will have to be accepted throughout the euro area wherever digital payments are possible, which will break the vicious circle in a way that private initiatives could not. Private payment providers will then have open rails on which to compete. Because a project of this scale takes years to build, we had to start well before the need became pressing. If the legislation is adopted by the end of this year, we aim to be ready for a first issuance in 2029. The second area was wholesale markets. With blockchain technology, securities can now be tokenised, so that they are issued, traded and settled on a single platform. With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity. But the window for seizing it is limited. The market for tokenised assets is still small, worth around €23 billion worldwide in March, but it was five times its size a year earlier. [ 4 ] As it grows, its standards and practices will take shape. If they develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. And as our capital markets have taught us, once standards and practices have diverged, they are very hard to bring back together. That is why, in September, we launched Pontes, which allows tokenised transactions to settle in central bank money on Eurosystem infrastructure, under European rules. Every platform now has access to a common settlement asset, so liquidity no longer has to be divided between them. Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism settled a €1 billion digitally native bond on Pontes. Through Appia, we are working with market participants towards an integrated European market, including common standards. But infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators. The third area was the international role of the euro. For most of its history, the ECB took a neutral view of the euro’s international role. Shortly before my term began, it moved to a more supportive line, and during my term we have acted on it. A stronger international role for the euro matters for our monetary policy, and it can support Europe’s growth and sovereignty in the world we now face. Europe faces large investment needs, from defence to the technologies on which our autonomy depends, and a currency that investors around the world want to hold lowers the cost of financing them. In a world of more frequent shocks, the more of our trade is invoiced in euro, the less exposed we are to swings in exchange rates. So, where it supports our own mandate, we have made the euro easier to use abroad. We are linking TIPS, our instant payment system, with fast payment systems in other regions. We have also strengthened our international liquidity lines as a backstop. In February we made EUREP, our repo facility for central banks, permanent and open to central banks worldwide. More than 30 central banks have already expressed interest. And we are working to keep our swap lines fit for purpose in a more fragmented world. They will be more accessible, too. The primary objective of these lines is to protect the transmission of our monetary policy in a crisis, by limiting spillovers from abroad into our own markets. But they also support the euro’s global role. A reserve manager who knows that euro securities can be turned into euro liquidity without a fire sale has more reason to hold them in normal times. What lessons can we draw? In our own field, we have tried to act on slow-moving risks early, before they were fully visible. I would draw three lessons from this experience. The first is that it is far easier to take the long view with a European mandate. I should be frank about our own case. If we were able to commit early, it was largely because of how we are built. Our mandate is defined for the euro area as a whole. Our horizon is long, and the Governing Council can decide by majority. That made our decisions easier than those facing national governments, which have to weigh concentrated opposition at home against benefits that are spread across Europe, while reaching agreement with partners who face the same constraints. But this is no reason for fatalism. It tells us something important about how Europe needs to be built. Where we agree that a challenge requires a European solution, we should strengthen the European institutions that can provide it, so that this trade-off weighs less heavily. In capital markets, that means a European supervisor able to take effective decisions. In technology, where projects such as chip plants and data centres need European scale, it means public-private partnerships at European level, with public money, including from the EU budget, taking the first losses and drawing in private capital. The second lesson is that we should design our response, wherever we can, so that it pays off even if the worst never happens. That makes it easier to build support for acting early, because we no longer need to agree on how likely the danger is. The digital euro is an example. Even if Europe is never cut off from the international card schemes, it will still be better placed, because we have designed the digital euro on open standards that allow any provider to offer services across the whole euro area. The same principle can guide other choices that require large commitments. Take defence. EU countries spent around €420 billion on defence last year, a fifth more than the year before, and are set to spend over €450 billion this year, [ 5 ] at a time when budgets are stretched and many other priorities compete for the same resources. But if more of that money is spent on research and development, it can benefit the whole economy, whatever the security outlook. Today, we spend ten times less on defence R&D than the United States, relative to the size of our economy. [ 6 ] Recent ECB analysis suggests that, over the long term, each additional euro of public R&D spending can generate almost 2.5 euros of GDP. [ 7 ] Not every choice can be designed this way. Some protection is simply insurance, and we should be honest that it has a price. But the more of our response we can design to pay off in every future, the easier it becomes to act in time. The third lesson is more personal. I have faced these decisions throughout my career as a policymaker, at national, European and international level. However carefully we design our choices, some uncertainty always remains, and someone has to take responsibility for deciding. The hardest judgement is to recognise when waiting has become the riskier choice, before the evidence is beyond doubt. At that point, leaders have to find the courage to make the case for acting, before a majority is ready to hear it. And those who act early must be prepared to go without thanks. As Henry Kissinger observed, “it is in the nature of successful policies that posterity forgets how easily things might have been otherwise.” So we should do everything we can to make acting early easier, by doing more at European level and by designing policies that pay off whatever the future holds. But we will also need leaders who believe in Europe and are prepared to fight for it. Conclusion Let me conclude. Over these seven years, I have seen Europe do things that were once thought impossible, when events had made the way ahead clear. The question now is whether it can act with the same resolve before the need becomes impossible to ignore. At the ECB, we have tried to do that in our own field. Whether we judged well, others will decide in time. But I hope I leave an institution that has helped give Europe more integration and more sovereignty than it had when I arrived. Much of what remains lies with others, and with those who will lead Europe in the years ahead. I am confident that they will find the conviction to act in time. Thank you. Schnitzer, M. et al.
