title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
body: November 20, 2026 Research Release Science Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates? Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next. Read the paper (opens in a new window) 00:00 Share We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines. One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing. MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model. What MedChemBench grades MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided. Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another. Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements. Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties. Prediction across competing properties One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay. Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay. Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown. The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly. 00:00 Small chemical changes can produce different property profiles. The task asks models to connect the structures with evidence about their behavior. Testing spatial reasoning in medicinal chemistry Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry. MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided. One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses. In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments. These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior. Figure 1. The same input, different molecules These selected answers for compound 17 show a correct reconstruction, a smaller ring, and disconnected fragments. While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks. We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens. Figure 2. Performance versus token usage Each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Tokens include reasoning and the final answer. The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain. Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism. Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices. Where we go from here These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field. 2026 Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Research acceleration: The jagged frontier Research Nov 18, 2026 Advancing chip design with OpenAI models Research Nov 18, 2026 Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Product Nov 17, 2026

title: Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT-6 Astra
body: November 20, 2026 Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT‑6 Astra Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra. Join the community Company size: Startup Region: North America Industry: Technology Products: API Required source types cited 13.6 Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested in Hebbia’s tests. Citation relevance 99.5 Percent of cited excerpts relevant to the question in Hebbia’s tests. Presentation requirements met 97.9 Percent of applicable presentation requirements met in Hebbia’s tests. Presentation requirement lead 14.4 Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested on presentation requirements. Share Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them. Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief. “We’ve been strong partners with OpenAI over the course of Hebbia’s lifetime, and the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in terms of quality outputs and accuracy have truly been surprising. GPT-6 Astra shines compared to any other model we’ve tested before on these two fronts.” —Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia From source documents to presentations It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template. In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines. “Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.” In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question. Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents. “When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says. A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client. “I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.” GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both. “In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says. In Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee. Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible: “What’s amazing about GPT-6 Astra is its ability to create really precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines. You can imagine the hours this will save professionals when you get a deck that is closer to your final output. The overnighters that you have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing GPT-6 Astra’s output.” —Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia A future role for agents Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess. “Imagine getting an important signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.” Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources. How to transfer your chat history into Gemini ICYMI: Transfer your history from other AI apps into Gemini. Nov 19, 2026 Switch to Gemini without starting from scratch. Here’s how to bring your context, preferences, and chat history from a different AI assistant into Gemini. Open your Gemini import settings and copy our prompt. Paste it into your previous AI tool to generate a summary of your preferences. Paste the response into Gemini. Export a ZIP file of your chat history from your previous provider's account settings. Upload the ZIP archive in Gemini settings to pick up conversations right where you left off. Posted in: Related stories Search Get your year-end tasks done with new Connected Apps. title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
body: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs NVIDIA and Microsoft expand tools for enterprises to customize AI models and deploy applications across cloud and local infrastructure. November 19, 2026 by Dave Salvator 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work. An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model , developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation. Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services. Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA. Visit NVIDIA at Ignite for demonstrations spanning enterprise applications, robotics, accelerated data processing and local computing, with hardware including an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack and RTX Spark devices. View NVIDIA sessions, hands-on labs and booth theater presentations . title: How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale.
body: How we’re putting one of quantum mechanics’ deepest features to the test at scale. Nov 19, 2026 Today, in new research published on the cover of Science , Google Quantum AI demonstrated that contextuality — a quantum property scientists believe powers certain quantum algorithms — survives at scale on our quantum processor. What gives quantum computers their unique power? While entanglement usually gets the spotlight, theory suggests that a deeper quantum property called contextuality may power certain quantum algorithms. In simple terms, contextuality means a system’s properties aren’t fixed in advance; what you measure depends on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it. Until recently, this effect had mostly been shown in small systems of just a few particles. Our paper in Science now demonstrates this at scale on our quantum processor. Using it, our qubits won a well-known coordination game 98.3% of the time, beating the 88.9% classical limit, and outperformed constrained classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits. These tests also serve as a sensitive new method to catch subtle hardware errors, helping pave the way for real-world applications like chemistry and materials science. Read the full Google Research blog post to learn more.

title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
body: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents See how developers are combining AI agents with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build simulation applications, test physical behavior and guide improvements. November 19, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Nyhamna_footage_take5_30s.mp4 AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions. Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation. AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view. Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream f or a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task. NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls. Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task. Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior. Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released. NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries : ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton , which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries. The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. Explore his open source demo f or build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills. Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/microducks-icu-pathtraced-16x9-1920x1080-1.mp4 Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting. AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours. Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗 Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

title: A smarter way to track and buy clean energy
body: A smarter way to track and buy clean energy Nov 19, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Granular certificates are a next-generation tool to ensure more accurate, impactful clean energy buying. Jenna Stauffer Head of Strategic Priorities, Climate Operations Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We are advancing Granular Certificates to track clean energy by hour and location, providing clear pricing signals that encourage smarter grid management. These tools help you match electricity use with local clean energy production, supporting a more stable power system. You can watch our new video to learn how these certificates help developers, energy asset owners, and the grid. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We use Granular Certificates to track clean energy supply by specific hour and geographic location. Trading volume in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic region increased 437% during our recent monthly spot auctions. Our support for the Registry Acceleration Fund helps organizations verify and track hourly energy data. These certificates provide new revenue streams for battery storage operators and improve grid stability overall. We reduced our Scope 2 emissions by 3% while managing a 37% increase in electricity load. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are using new tools called Granular Certificates to track clean energy by the hour and location. These certificates help us match our electricity use with local solar or wind power, even when the sun is not shining. By creating clear price signals, this system encourages companies to build more batteries and clean energy projects where they are needed most. This helps us manage our power use and supports a cleaner, more stable energy grid. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Granular Certificates (GCs) are next-generation clean energy instruments. They precisely track supply by hour and location, helping companies match their electricity load with local clean energy. Their hourly pricing signals encourage the development of clean generation and energy storage when and where it is needed most. These instruments can incentivize improved grid management, and they can help accelerate the deployment of advanced clean technologies, leading to a cleaner, more stable power system. But like any nascent solution, the foundational building blocks need to be in place first. We first started piloting GCs in 2021 and, in just five years, they’ve transitioned from early concept to real-world certificates, traded on specific hours. We’re continuing to take actions to accelerate both our own procurement and the global GC ecosystem. Here are three key ways the GC ecosystem advanced this year: 1. The GC marketplace is growing. Marketplaces are critical because they establish transparent hourly pricing signals and help simplify processes for those new to hourly procurement. LevelTen, in partnership with the Granular Certificate Trading Alliance (GCTA) and the Intercontinental Exchange, launched the Granular Certificate Marketplace in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic grid region PJM in October 2025. Since that first auction, trading volume has increased 437% in just one year , with Google participating in every monthly spot auction. This increased trading volume generates clear pricing signals, with higher premiums occurring during evening hours. By demonstrating when buyers need clean energy most, GCs can incentivize suppliers to operate or build clean energy to meet this demand. 2. Global registries help with tracking and verification. Almost every corporate clean energy buyer uses registries, which track and verify their clean energy purchases via instruments like monthly or annual energy attribute certificates (EACs). Registries help also ensure EACs are not double counted, supporting unique clean energy claims. However, until recently, the vast majority of registries didn’t have the technical capabilities to accommodate GCs. To help address those gaps, Google supported the GCTA in establishing the Registry Acceleration Fund . The fund awarded grants to five of the largest organizations that operate registries, which collectively issue or track 4,000 TWh of certificates in over 70+ countries. As of today, one of these organizations has met their technical milestones that would allow them to transfer, verify, and retire GCs. The remaining four organizations are expected to finish in early 2027. This will add critical functionality needed for these instruments to scale, including standardization of the hourly data and traceability to one clear owner. 3. GCs are driving real value. Despite the GC market’s nascency, its potential benefits are moving from academic research concepts towards demonstrating real impact. For example, in a recent GCTA white paper , clean energy developers and asset operators shared real-life perspectives on granular matching. These developers explained that pricing signals from GCs can help them maximize existing energy assets in the near-term, while helping them make crucial decisions about project siting and technology diversification in the longer term. In addition, Google, esVolta, Quintrace, and LevelTen helped prove a new revenue stream for battery energy storage system operators. We partnered to pilot the first GCs for storage systems, shifting solar generation to match our targeted demand hours. This could not have happened without hourly tracking and verification via GCs. Hear more firsthand accounts of the benefits of GCs to developers, energy asset owners, and the grid in our new video . In addition to the maturing global ecosystem, we’ve also continued to evolve our use of GCs to help manage Google’s emissions. We’ll always prioritize applying new, long-term clean energy agreements, and the underlying hourly GCs, first. Even with a large clean energy portfolio, the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow exactly when we need it to. Marketplace GCs help fill those gaps. At the same time, our purchases help build a stronger market where GCs can be bought and sold quickly, easily, and in large quantities — creating clearer price signals and providing granular options for growing numbers of buyers. We used a smaller amount of marketplace GCs alongside a much larger amount of clean energy agreements to help lower our Scope 2 market-based emissions by 3% from 2024 to 2025 , despite a 37% electricity load increase. We will include a limited amount of marketplace GCs in our 24/7 CFE performance in the future. Looking ahead, these tools will become even more important to develop. The recently released net zero standard of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) will require reporting on hourly matching performance for large energy users, and the GHG Protocol (GHGP) is evaluating the introduction of hourly emissions reporting. We will continue to work on developing and advancing GCs — not just for our own efforts, but to ensure others can use these tools to build a better energy system. body: Genie 4 is now available on the Gemini API. Nov 19, 2026 Following yesterday's Genie 4 launch , Genie 4 is now available for developers through the Gemini API (via the Interactions API) and Google AI Studio . Starting from a text prompt, a reference image, or both, developers can experiment with generating continuous 720p worlds at 24fps with synchronized native audio — from ambient soundscapes and sound effects to character dialogue. Using real-time keyboard controls alongside live text prompts, you can navigate environments and change weather, lighting, objects, or events on the fly. Gemini reasoning keeps the world state consistent and coherent throughout. Whether you’re prototyping interactive experiences, visualizing designs for spatial concepts, or training robotics and AI agents, Genie 4 opens up a blank canvas for you to test ideas and define new possibilities. As a reminder every output includes imperceptible SynthID watermarking. Try the interactive canvas and starter apps in Google AI Studio . Review pricing details and explore the Gemini API documentation to begin building.

title: Build strategic A/B tests to grow your ad performance.
body: Google Ads Build strategic A/B tests to grow your ad performance. Nov 19, 2026 In an era of rapid AI innovation, experimentation can serve as a strategic compass. In the latest episode of Ads Decoded, Ads Product Liaison Ginny Marvin sits down with product leads Sagar Shah and Al Nevarez to explore how A/B testing validates AI Max features, budget shifts, and Smart Bidding strategies. Three key rules to guide your testing: Start with templated setups: Pre-built templates isolate single variables, split traffic 50/50, and minimize setup errors for cleaner data. Focus on business outcomes: Measure qualified conversions rather than shallow proxies, and give tests four to six weeks to account for conversion lag. Match confidence to decision scope: An 80% confidence interval works well for directional tweaks. Reserve 95% certainty for major structural overhauls. Explore the Experiments tab in Google Ads, test with confidence, and let data prove the value before scaling. Listen here.
